headline: US stocks slide as volatility jumps and credit holds up
summary: The S&P 500 fell 2.02% to 7,175.83, its sixth straight decline. The Nasdaq Composite lost 2.25%, the Dow 2.19% and the Russell 2000 2.18%. All 11 S&P sectors fell, and NYSE decliners outnumbered advancers 2,339 to 515. Equal-weight stocks held up a little better than the cap-weighted benchmark, but they still fell 1.76%. That distinction matters: megacap weakness amplified the decline, but it does not explain a session in which small caps, semiconductors and defensive shares all finished lower.

highlights.title: AI demand did not translate into support for AI shares
highlights.text: Anthropic closed its first session at US$97.17, up 17.1% from its offer but below its US$111.50 opening trade. The drop from the open tells more about the shift in appetite than the gain from the offer. The semiconductor index fell 2.41%, and 19 of 20 stocks in the report’s sample closed in the bottom quarter of their daily ranges. That suggests a broad repricing of AI exposure; it does not prove investors sold other AI stocks to fund IPO purchases.

highlights.title: Equity stress did not spread decisively to credit
highlights.text: The dollar firmed while gold and copper fell, but two-year and ten-year Treasury yields both declined. High-yield and investment-grade bond ETFs slipped just 0.16% and 0.07%. That points more to pressure on equity valuations than to an abrupt funding squeeze or a sell-off driven by rising yields. Defensive sectors fell too, offering little evidence that investors simply rotated from technology into staples and utilities.

highlights.title: What would change the view
highlights.text: Watch whether equal-weight and small-cap shares recover alongside the headline index and whether NYSE breadth returns towards parity. Friday’s options expiry can amplify a move without resolving whether demand has broadened. A rebound confined to megacaps, with near-term volatility still elevated, would be weak evidence of a turn. Further equity losses with more pronounced weakness in both credit ETFs would make the funding-stress explanation more credible.

highlights.title: After-hours earnings are a separate signal
highlights.text: Intuit and Elastic weakened after the bell, according to the report. Those moves did not contribute to the cash-session index declines. The next test is whether weakness carries into regular trading and broadens across software, or stays confined to companies reporting results. If chip and software names both lag on firmer market breadth, that would be stronger evidence of an AI-specific repricing than Thursday’s across-the-board decline.

highlights.title: Market sentiment: protection demand rises, retail signals stay mixed
highlights.text: Nine-day implied volatility reached 29.26, above the VIX at 28.44 and the three-month reading at 27.03. That inversion points to near-term stress. Eight of 14 comments from selected market observers were cautious, against one constructive. Retail signals were mixed: AAII bearishness eased to 42.2% from 51.4%, but the survey closed before the sell-off. Online discussion was mixed and does not measure orders. Volatility and weak breadth were stronger evidence of caution.

forecast.outlook: Upside has the largest weight; downside is close behind
forecast.horizon: 20–24 November US sessions · S&P 500 final close
forecast.method: Original NEW section 3.1 card. Averages three non-independent estimates and includes a −0.0139% ES adjustment. Base includes both endpoints. Sentiment does not adjust the probabilities.
forecast.watch_next: Watch Friday’s options expiry, breadth, short-dated volatility and credit.

limitations: No verified timestamped SPX options chain. Event risk was not modelled separately. The 14 scored windows overlap, and only the latest was reread from its original for this report; the sample does not establish calibration.
